##                                                                                          30.4 
##                                                               China, excluding diverted chips 
##                                                                                           4.5 
##                      the rate in years four to seven on that assumption (% a year, mid-year)1 
##                                                                                           1.9 
##                      the rate in years four to seven on that assumption (% a year, mid-year)2 
##                                                                                           4.9 
##                      the rate in years four to seven on that assumption (% a year, mid-year)3 
##                                                                                           7.9 
##                      the rate in years four to seven on that assumption (% a year, mid-year)4 
##                                                                                          10.9
  • Failed chips. A chip that fails under warranty goes back to the vendor, which keeps the return under its serial number, so it rarely goes missing (the census of §S.6.5 takes 1% of these failures to leave no record). Accelerators are sold in servers that typically remain under warranty for three years (NVIDIA 2026c; Dell Technologies 2026; Hewlett Packard Enterprise 2026); the terms large operators negotiate with their manufacturers are not public. A failure after the warranty has run out could be scrapped with no record outside the owner’s own, and few chips are old enough for that: about 4.9k H100e in the U.S. (1.8–10.4k) and about 0.8k in China. That is an upper bound, since large owners scrap through certified recyclers. Those figures hold the measured rate at every age. The rate was measured on chips under three years old, and nothing measures these chips later in life, so the census of §S.6.5 takes a less favorable assumption: the measured rate to year three, then three percentage points more per year for each further year of age (about 2% in year four and 11% in year seven). That is a judgmental input with no source, chosen to err on the regime-unfavorable side. On it the failures after warranty are about 30k H100e in the U.S. and 4.5k in China. Chips diverted around U.S. export controls are a separate case: they carry no warranty, so none of their failures has a vendor record (§S.6.5).
  • Retired chips. None yet (§S.1.2.6). After the agreement, licensed operators destroy retired chips verifiably, so retirement does not become a channel for losing them.
  • No data found for two further lines. (i) Customers of record that no longer exist, and undocumented resale: a secondary market exists (a marketplace for used H100s and A100s opened in July 2026 reporting requests “from hundreds to tens of thousands of GPUs”; used H100s trade at roughly $18–22k), but no source gives its volume, and chips this young and supply-constrained have mostly stayed with their first owners. (ii) Diverters’ unshipped inventory: chips held by shell companies on the day the agreement takes effect; at the §S.1.2.8 diversion flow of about 0.3–0.5M H100e a year and a dwell time of one to three months (a guess), 30–120k worldwide, mostly in third countries.

Reading. On this definition the one line that can be computed is failures after the warranty, about 30k H100e in the U.S. and 4.5k in China on the rising rate, of which the census takes a tenth to leave no record (§S.6.5). What a census would miss beyond that lies in the lines that cannot, above all chips in the long tail of owners that are neither declared nor traced through records; §S.6.4 and §S.6.5 estimate that by holding type. Most of the genuinely dark stock is the diverted stock, counted separately. Two independent checks bound what a state could conceal by under-declaring production rather than holdings: lithography-tool usage records held by the tool and laser vendors, and above all high-bandwidth-memory shipments, which go almost entirely into accelerators at a fixed number of stacks per package (Patel, AJ, and Xie 2025: “13 million stacks of HBM” reached China before the December 2024 controls, enough for “1.6M Ascend 910C packages”; Chinese-made memory from 2026 on is outside foreign ledgers, and about half of Huawei’s 2026 units are 950PRs built on “non-HBM DRAM” for the prefill stage of inference (Somala 2026), which the memory check does not see at all).

S.6.4 Who holds the stock: named owners, the unnamed residual, and China’s true tail

A census does two jobs (§3.3.2): it gets most chips declared, and it classifies and quantifies what is not. Both depend on who holds the chips. Owners with a sourced, individually documented holding (company filings and releases, government budgets, press reports of specific clusters, and Epoch’s data-center hub, Epoch AI 2026g) are called named owners. Like the seven large U.S. firms, they are presumed accounted for: audited books or public budgets, known sites, and chips that report their identity when running. The two lists are in data/large_owners_us.csv (75 rows) and data/large_owners_cn.csv (18 rows); each row carries its source and the basis of its number, and the census counts the rows marked in_tally = y. Every link in the two lists was opened and compared with its row on October 9, 2026. Rows that this check could not confirm, and that the authors did not then review themselves, are not counted and are left out of the published lists. Holdings are in Epoch’s H100e. A holding counts from the date of its evidence, so the end-2025 figures are floors.

own.c <- read.csv("data/ai_chip_owners_cumulative_by_designer.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
a100.n <- sum(a100.pre$h)                                                                                     # A100s sold before 2022 (section S.1.2.1)
nd.c <- function(e) { x <- own.c[own.c[["End date"]] == e, ]; sum(x[x$Owner == "Other", Hcol]) - sum(x[x$Owner == "China (smuggled)", Hcol]) + a100.mix[["Other"]] * a100.n }   # 'Other' less diverted
wd.c <- function(e) { x <- own.c[own.c[["End date"]] == e, ]; sum(x[x$Owner != "China (smuggled)", Hcol]) + a100.n }                                         # world, no diverted row
lo.us <- read.csv("data/large_owners_us.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE); lo.us <- lo.us[lo.us$in_tally == "y", ]
lo.cn <- read.csv("data/large_owners_cn.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE); lo.cn <- lo.cn[lo.cn$in_tally == "y", ]
held.at <- function(r, q) {       # a holding at quarter-end q: its dated milestones, or its end-2025 value from its install date
  pts <- if (nzchar(r$ms)) do.call(rbind, lapply(strsplit(strsplit(r$ms, ";")[[1]], ":"), function(z) data.frame(t = as.numeric(z[1]), v = as.numeric(z[2]))))
         else data.frame(t = numeric(0), v = numeric(0))
  if (!nzchar(r$ms)) { if (r$e25 > 0) pts <- rbind(pts, data.frame(t = ifelse(is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(r$t0))), 2026, as.numeric(r$t0)), v = r$e25))
                       if (r$firm > max(c(0, pts$v))) pts <- rbind(pts, data.frame(t = 2026.75, v = r$firm)) }
  z <- pts[pts$t <= q + 1e-9, ]; if (nrow(z)) z$v[which.max(z$t)] else 0 }
named.us <- sapply(c(2024, 2025, 2026), function(q) sum(sapply(seq_len(nrow(lo.us)), function(i) held.at(lo.us[i, ], q))))
ends  <- c("2023-12-31", "2024-12-31", "2025-12-31")
tw    <- sapply(ends, nd.c) - named.us; ww <- sapply(ends, wd.c)
s.add <- mean(diff(tw) / diff(ww))                               # the unnamed tail's share of world additions, 2024 and 2025
tail25.us <- other.us.loc * nd.c("2025-12-31") - named.us[3]      # unnamed U.S. residual, end-2025
g.u   <- 1 + s.add * (fleet.ye2026 - ww[3]) / tw[3]              # 2026 growth: it keeps its share of world additions
N.us  <- unname(tail25.us * g.u)
## China: official stock (diverted chips excluded) = named + unnamed large buyers + true tail
ct.c <- read.csv("data/ai_chip_owners_cumulative_by_chip_type.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
ct.c <- ct.c[ct.c$Owner == "China" & ct.c[["End date"]] == "2025-12-31", ]; stk.cn <- setNames(ct.c[[Hcol]], ct.c[["Chip type"]])
stk.cn[["A100"]] <- stk.cn[["A100"]] + a100.mix[["China"]] * a100.n
cn.official <- china.fleet.ye2026 - smuggled.ye2026
large.share <- c(H20 = 0.80, A800 = 0.83, H800 = 0.53, A100 = 0.53, `Instinct MI308X` = 0)
big.cn <- max(0, sum(large.share * stk.cn[names(large.share)]) - sum(lo.cn$sched[grepl("A100|A800|H800|Hopper|H20 assumed|6,500 GPUs", lo.cn$basis)])) +
          max(0, 0.79 * (stk.cn[["Siyuan 590"]] + 4 * 0.01e6) - sum(lo.cn$sched[grepl("Siyuan 590", lo.cn$basis)]))
tail.cn <- cn.official - sum(lo.cn$sched) - big.cn
cbind(value = round(c("U.S.: named owners' holdings, end-2023 (k)" = named.us[1] / 1e3, "  end-2024 (k)" = named.us[2] / 1e3, "  end-2025 (k)" = named.us[3] / 1e3,
    "  year-end 2026, including deliveries due in 2026 (M)" = sum(lo.us$sched) / 1e6,
    "U.S.: the unnamed tail's share of world additions, 2024 (%)" = 100 * unname(diff(tw) / diff(ww))[1], "  2025 (%)" = 100 * unname(diff(tw) / diff(ww))[2],
    "U.S.: unnamed residual, end-2025 (M)" = tail25.us / 1e6, "  2026 growth factor" = unname(g.u), "  year-end 2026 (M)" = unname(N.us) / 1e6,
    "China: official stock, end-2025 (M)" = sum(stk.cn) / 1e6, "  year-end 2026 (M)" = cn.official / 1e6,
    "China: named owners, end-2025 (M)" = sum(lo.cn$e25) / 1e6, "  year-end 2026 (M)" = sum(lo.cn$sched) / 1e6,
    "China: unnamed large buyers, year-end 2026 (M)" = big.cn / 1e6, "China: true tail, year-end 2026 (M)" = tail.cn / 1e6), 3))

  • The U.S. Named owners outside the seven firms hold 0.29M H100e dated to end-2025 and 1.0M at year-end 2026 if the deliveries they announce for 2026 arrive: Tesla, the Department of Energy’s laboratories, neoclouds (Nscale, Lightning AI, Lambda), universities. The unnamed residual is what is left of the non-hyperscale stock of §S.6.1 once they are subtracted: 0.96M at end-2025. It grows in 2026 by keeping the share of world additions that the stock outside the seven firms, China and the named owners took in 2024 and 2025 (11%), a factor of 2.2, to 2.1M at year-end 2026. Two alternatives bracket it: no 2026 purchases (0.96M) and the 2025 growth factor carried forward (about 2.3M), which would outgrow the world stock.
  • China. Epoch does not name Chinese owners, so the list was built from filings, tenders and press reports: the telecom operators’ owned capacity (China Mobile’s self-built 33 EFLOPS, China Telecom’s 71 EFLOPS, China Unicom’s 45 EFLOPS of unstated precision, counted at half), Huawei’s Horinger campus and a VNET campus in Ulanqab (estimates from Epoch’s data-center hub; Epoch AI 2026g), ByteDance (third-party estimates of its purchases), Alibaba’s Zhangbei site, city and national computing centres, and AI labs. Named holdings are 0.33M at end-2025 (28% of the official stock) and 0.45M at year-end 2026. Capacity stated in FP16 converts at 1 H100e per PFLOPS; capacity of unstated precision at 0.5 (the regime-unfavorable reading, since fewer named chips leave a larger tail).
  • Unnamed large buyers. NVIDIA’s China-specific chips went mostly to a few buyers: ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent and Baidu took more than 80% of 2024 H20 demand (a Bernstein estimate, as reported by Sina Finance 2025); four firms ordered about 100,000 A800s for 2023 delivery, 83% of Epoch’s total (Reuters 2023); ByteDance alone had about 100,000 A100 and H800 delivered or on order in mid-2023, 53% of those two chips (IT Home 2023, citing LatePost). Cambricon’s largest customer took 79% of its 2024 revenue (Cambricon Technologies 2025). Those shares, less the named holdings of the same chips, give 0.28M. Ascend (about three quarters of the year-end 2026 official stock) has no buyer data, so its unnamed part is all counted as tail: the true tail is 1.4M. That is the regime-unfavorable reading.

S.6.5 What a census would miss, by holding type (§5.5)

The missing stock \(K_M(s)\) in state \(s\) is what a census conducted in good faith fails to find. Each state’s stock is sorted into four holding types \(h\), with \(Q(h, s)\) the stock of type \(h\). Failed chips are taken out of each type first, and a share of them is missing because no record shows that they failed. A missing fraction \(\mu(h)\) then applies to the functional chips that remain:

\[K_M(s) \;=\; \sum_h \Big[\,D(h, s) \;+\; \mu(h)\,\big(Q(h, s) - \text{failed chips}(h, s)\big)\Big],\]

where \(D(h, s)\) is the number of failed chips that go missing, the paper’s symbol.

The four holding types, in decreasing order of visibility:

  • Publicly identifiable holdings: the seven large U.S. firms, the named owners of §S.6.4 and, in China, the named owners and the unnamed large buyers.
  • On-books business and institutional holdings: firms, laboratories and smaller clouds that hold chips on their books and appear in the chain of sales records, but are not individually documented here. In the U.S. this is the unnamed residual less its informal part; in China, the true tail less its informal part, plus the diverted chips whose holders have some state record, such as a customs entry or a tax invoice.
  • Off-books business and institutional holdings: chips bought without paperwork and run by an operating business or institution. Only China’s diverted stock has these.
  • Informal holdings: individuals, and the shell companies and traders engaged in diversion, with their stock in transit.

Every rate below is a judgment or an analogy from another domain, chosen for its structure, with the direction of its bias stated.

d.F <- 0.94; p.T <- 0.80                                     # on-books holdings: declaration, tracing
d.IS <- 0.80; p.IS <- 0.50                                   # off-books and informal holdings: declaration, recovery (judgmental inputs)
v.off <- 0.01                                                # share of the stock not publicly identifiable that is held informally, in both states
out.dc <- 0.10; miss.dc <- 0.06                                # business-held chips outside a data center; chips in a data center that its operator's declaration and an inspection both miss
f.site <- out.dc + miss.dc                                     # share of business-held chips not found at a site
srv <- rbind("2023" = c(small = 8.5, hyperscale = 30.0), "2025" = c(small = 6.4, hyperscale = 34.8))   # % of U.S. servers, measured from Figure 4.1 of Shehabi et al. (2024)
venue <- c(enterprise.dc = 45, colocation = 16, closet.edge = 14) / 75      # for comparison: operators' own IT by venue (Uptime Institute 2025, Figure 13)
mu <- c(0, (1 - d.F) * (1 - p.T) * f.site, (1 - d.IS) * (1 - p.IS) * f.site, (1 - d.IS) * (1 - p.IS))   # missing fraction of functional chips, by holding type
w.in <- 0.01; w.out <- 0.10; w.off <- 0.50                     # failed chips with no record made at the time: under warranty, after it, at off-books holdings (all at informal holdings)
## failed chips as a share of each group's year-end 2026 stock: at any age, and after the three-year warranty
oq.o <- read.csv("data/ai_chip_owners_quarters_by_chip_type.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE); oq.o <- oq.o[oq.o[["Start date"]] <= "2025-12-31", ]
oq.o$t <- as.numeric(substr(oq.o[["Start date"]], 1, 4)) + (as.numeric(substr(oq.o[["Start date"]], 6, 7)) - 1) %/% 3 / 4 + 0.125
oq.o$h <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(oq.o[[Hcol]])); oq.o <- oq.o[!is.na(oq.o$h), c("Owner", "t", "h")]
oq.o <- rbind(oq.o, do.call(rbind, lapply(names(a100.mix), function(o) data.frame(Owner = o, t = a100.pre$t, h = a100.mix[[o]] * a100.pre$h))))   # with the A100s sold before 2022
oow.c <- function(x, w = 3) { a <- 2027 - x$t; sum((x$h * (exp(-Hz(w)) - exp(-Hz(a))))[a > w]) }          # Hz: the rate rises after year three (S.6.3)
x7 <- oq.o[oq.o$Owner %in% us.seven, ]; xo <- oq.o[oq.o$Owner == "Other", ]; xc <- oq.o[oq.o$Owner == "China", ]
## the 2026 vintage: Epoch's owner data end in 2025, so each group's 2026 additions (its year-end 2026 stock less its end-2025 stock) are added,
## spread over the four quarters in proportion to the world model's quarterly flow
wq26 <- c(stock.q2 - q2f - ww[[3]], world.q$flow[1:3]); wq26 <- wq26 / sum(wq26); t26 <- 2026 + c(0.125, 0.375, 0.625, 0.875)
add26 <- function(x, tot) rbind(x[, c("t", "h")], data.frame(t = t26, h = max(tot, 0) * wq26))
s7 <- sum(x7$h)                                                                                               # the seven firms' end-2025 stock
x7 <- add26(x7, s7 * (fleet.ye2026 / ww[[3]] - 1)); xo <- add26(xo, other.share * (fleet.ye2026 - ww[[3]])); xc <- add26(xc, cn.official - sum(xc$h))
dv <- data.frame(t = 2024 + (0:11) / 4 + 0.125, h = smuggled.ye2026 / 12)          # diverted chips: the straight line from zero at the start of 2024
fail <- rbind(seven    = c(all = oow.c(x7, 0), late = oow.c(x7)) / (s7 * fleet.ye2026 / ww[[3]]),     # the seven keep their share of the world stock in 2026
              other    = c(all = oow.c(xo, 0), late = oow.c(xo)) / (other.share * fleet.ye2026),
              china    = c(all = oow.c(xc, 0), late = oow.c(xc)) / cn.official,
              diverted = c(all = oow.c(dv, 0), late = oow.c(dv, 0)) / smuggled.ye2026)                        # no warranty: every failure counts as after it
off.div <- 0.10; transit <- smuggled.2025 / 2 / 12             # a tenth of the diverted stock off the books; one month of diverted flow at Epoch's central rate for 2024-25, in transit
named.us26 <- sum(lo.us$sched); N7 <- us.fleet.ye2026 - N.us - named.us26; named.cn <- sum(lo.cn$sched) + big.cn
cell <- function(Q, g, win, wout, nowarranty = FALSE) { all <- Q * fail[[g, "all"]]; late <- if (nowarranty) all else Q * fail[[g, "late"]]
  c(Q = Q, failed = all, miss.failed = win * (all - late) + wout * late) }
hl <- c("publicly identifiable holdings", "on-books holdings", "off-books holdings", "informal holdings")
fin <- function(m) { dimnames(m) <- list(hl, c("Q", "failed", "miss.failed")); fun <- m[, "Q"] - m[, "failed"]
  cbind(m, functional = fun, mu = mu, miss.fun = mu * fun, missing = m[, "miss.failed"] + mu * fun) }
hold.us <- fin(rbind(cell(N7, "seven", w.in, w.out) + cell(named.us26, "other", w.in, w.out),
                     cell((1 - v.off) * N.us, "other", w.in, w.out), c(0, 0, 0),
                     cell(v.off * N.us, "other", 1, 1) + c(transit / 2, 0, 0)))                               # stock in transit has not failed
hold.cn <- fin(rbind(cell(named.cn, "china", w.in, w.out),
                     cell((1 - v.off) * tail.cn, "china", w.in, w.out) + cell((1 - off.div - v.off) * smuggled.ye2026, "diverted", w.out, w.out, TRUE),
                     cell(off.div * smuggled.ye2026, "diverted", w.off, w.off, TRUE),
                     cell(v.off * tail.cn, "china", 1, 1) + cell(v.off * smuggled.ye2026, "diverted", 1, 1, TRUE) + c(transit / 2, 0, 0)))
K.miss.us <- sum(hold.us[, "missing"]); K.miss.cn <- sum(hold.cn[, "missing"])
div.miss <- function(off = off.div, D = smuggled.ye2026) { fd <- fail[["diverted", "all"]]                    # what the diverted stock adds to China's missing stock
  D * ((1 - off - v.off) * (w.out * fd + mu[2] * (1 - fd)) + off * (w.off * fd + mu[3] * (1 - fd)) + v.off * (fd + mu[4] * (1 - fd))) }
signif(100 * fail, 3)        # failed, % of the year-end 2026 stock: all failures, and those after the warranty
##            all   late
## seven    0.521 0.0644
## other    0.763 0.1880
## china    0.803 0.2120

tab <- function(m) cbind("Q (k H100e)" = round(m[, "Q"] / 1e3), "failed (k)" = round(m[, "failed"] / 1e3, 2), "failed chips missing (k)" = round(m[, "miss.failed"] / 1e3, 2),
                         "functional (k)" = round(m[, "functional"] / 1e3), "mu (%)" = signif(100 * m[, "mu"], 2), "functional missing (k)" = round(m[, "miss.fun"] / 1e3, 2),
                         "total missing (k)" = round(m[, "missing"] / 1e3, 2))
tab(hold.us); tab(hold.cn)

The formula as the paper states it. The paper states the formula with \(\mu(h)\) applied to the whole stock \(Q(h, s)\) and notes (its footnote 53) that this makes no difference; the table above, like the paper’s Table 5.1, applies it to the functional chips. Failed chips are at most 0.8% of any group, and applying \(\mu(h)\) to the whole stock would add 47 H100e to the U.S. total and 61 to China’s.

Failed chips, and how many of them are missing

  • How many have failed. By year-end 2026, 0.52% of the seven firms’ stock has failed at some age, 0.76% of other U.S. holders’, 0.8% of China’s non-diverted stock and 0.67% of the diverted stock, which has a mean age of 1.5 years. The rate is the measured one to year three and rises by three percentage points a year after it (§S.6.3), which is on the regime-unfavorable side. Purchases are dated by quarter: through 2025 from Epoch’s owner data, and for 2026, which Epoch’s owner data do not yet cover, from each group’s additions in the world model, spread over the year’s quarters in proportion to the world flow. In all, 190k H100e of the U.S. stock and 24k of China’s have failed.
  • Under warranty: 1% missing. A chip that fails within its three-year warranty goes back to the vendor, which records the return (§S.6.3). At publicly identifiable and on-books holdings, 1% of these failures are taken to leave no record, the vendor’s or any other made at the time. That is a judgment.
  • After the warranty: 10% missing. Only chips bought before 2024 can have failed after year three: 0.064% of the seven firms’ year-end 2026 stock, 0.19% of other U.S. holders’ and 0.21% of China’s non-diverted stock. Any record made at the time that the chip failed and was taken out of service counts: a maintenance ticket or monitoring log, an entry in the holder’s inventory, a write-off in its books, or a recycler’s disposal record (China’s rules on waste electrical and electronic products require licensed disposal enterprises to keep data on what they process for three years; State Council of the People’s Republic of China 2009). A disposal certificate is not required. A tenth of these failures are taken to leave no record of any of these kinds. That is a judgment: no rule requires a record when an accelerator fails, and nothing measures how often one is kept. An operator that monitors its machines learns of a failure from its own logs, which is where the measured failure rate itself comes from (Cui et al. 2025), so a tenth is probably on the high side for data-center operators and less certain for a small business with a few machines.
  • Diverted chips have no warranty (NVIDIA provides no support or repairs for restricted products; Olcott 2026a), so every failure of a diverted chip held on the books is counted at the after-warranty share, a tenth.
  • Off-books holdings: half missing. Informal holdings: all. Both are judgments. A business running chips bought without paperwork still keeps operating records, taken to show half of its failures. An informal holder has nothing to show, so all of its failures count, inside the warranty period or after it.
  • In all, the missing failed chips are 4.5k H100e in the U.S. and 1.7k in China. The U.S. figure is the larger because of the size of its publicly identifiable holdings, which account for 3.8k of it.

Functional chips: the missing fraction

A functional chip goes missing only if three things happen in turn: it is not found at a site; of the chips not found there, its holder does not declare it; and of those not found and not declared, the census cannot trace it from the seller’s records. The rates below are conditional in that order, as the paper states them (§5.5.2).

  • Publicly identifiable holdings: none. Their functional chips are presumed accounted for: public filings, vendor records, known sites, chips that report their identity when running. The failed chips above are this type’s whole contribution. Chips these holders have resold are not counted: the stock counts purchases, and nothing public measures the secondary market.
  • The site: 16% not found. A chip that escapes the paper trail but sits at an operating business is still found if it is in a data center: a colocation operator declares its tenants and their power by cage, and an enterprise data center is a known site from utility and permit records that the census can inspect. Two inputs set the share that is not found. A tenth of business-held chips are taken to sit outside any data center, in closets, server rooms, edge sites and small businesses’ own premises. Counted by racks, 8.5% of U.S. servers sat in such places in 2023 and 6.4% in 2025; of the servers outside hyperscale facilities, the closer comparison for holders that are not named, 12% and 10% (Shehabi et al. 2024, Figure 4.1, measured from the chart). That is all servers, not AI servers, whose power density keeps most of them out of closets; the same report’s model places every AI-accelerated server in a hyperscale or large colocation facility. So a tenth is on the regime-unfavorable side. A survey of data-center operators gives a higher figure, 19% of the IT on their own hardware (Uptime Institute 2025, Figure 13), but it averages over the operators who answered, not over hardware. A further 6% are taken to be in a data center and still missed, by its operator’s declaration and by its owner’s; the figure borrows the IRS rate below. The two are added, giving 16%; applying the 6% only to the nine tenths inside a data center would give 15.4%. Informal holdings have no site to inspect.
  • Undeclared, on the books: 6%. A business that bought a chip is the end of a chain of sales records. The IRS measures that 6% of income subject to substantial third-party information reporting goes unreported (category II; Internal Revenue Service 2024, p. 16), which is used for \(d_F\) = 0.94. The analogy overstates non-declaration: the IRS measures misreporting where it saves tax, whereas a chip is a capital asset already in the holder’s books and on its tax return, and under the regime declaring earns licensed use or a buyback while an undeclared chip is contraband. A business has little reason not to declare; the 6% stands for the declaration channel failing, through error or a defunct holder, and is the regime-unfavorable reading.
  • Untraced, on the books: 20%. An ATF trace follows a gun’s serial forward from the manufacturer through wholesaler and dealer to the first retail buyer; it reached the buyer in 77% of traces over 2017–21 and 80% in 2021 (Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives 2023), which is used for the tracing rate \(p_T\) = 0.80. Crime guns are older and more often resold than these chips, so this analogy too is on the regime-unfavorable side.
  • Off the books and informal: 20% undeclared, half of those not recovered. Both are judgmental inputs; no measurement applies to a holder whose purchase is off the books. Such a holder can keep a chip for the black market more easily than one whose purchase is in the tax record, so more go undeclared. With no sales record to trace from, recovery rests on other records (power, employees, customers) and on tips, taken to find half.
  • So the missing fraction of functional chips is 0.19% for on-books holdings (16% × 6% × 20%), 1.6% for off-books holdings (16% × 20% × 50%) and 10% for informal holdings (20% × 50%).

How each state’s stock is sorted

  • The U.S. The seven firms and the named owners are publicly identifiable holdings, 33M H100e. Of the unnamed residual (2.1M), 1% is taken to be held informally, a judgment that nothing measures; no evidence was found of individuals holding data-center GPUs in quantity. The rest is on the books.
  • China’s non-diverted stock. Named owners and unnamed large buyers are publicly identifiable holdings, 730k; the true tail is split as the U.S. residual is.
  • China’s diverted stock (0.99M: Epoch’s central estimate through 2025, carried a third year, §S.1.2.8; the same stock as everywhere else in this supplement). A tenth is taken to be off the books, 99k, and 1% informal, as for any stock that is not publicly identifiable. The remaining 89% is on the books (a customs entry, a tax invoice, a tender, a financing filing). The tenth is a judgment, meant to err on the high side, since a firm has to hold the invoice to claim the tax credit; the evidence behind it follows.
  • Stock in transit. One month of diverted flow at Epoch’s central rate for 2024–25 (0.66M over two years, the rate at which the stock is carried through 2026, so 28k H100e a month) is taken to be with shell companies and traders on the pause date. Half of it is added to each state’s informal holdings. It is new stock, so none of it has failed.

Why only a tenth of the diverted stock is taken to be off Chinese records

No source measures the share. Four kinds of evidence bear on it.

cl <- read.csv("data/customs_server_lanes.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE); hk.c <- read.csv("data/hk_server_imports_by_consignment.csv")
cv <- function(rep, flow, code, partner, from, to, col = "value_usd")
  sum(cl[[col]][cl$reporter == rep & cl$flow == flow & cl$code_hs6 == code & cl$partner == partner & cl$period >= from & cl$period <= to])
## China's own import record, servers (HS 847150) at AI-server prices: Malaysia (Epoch's corridor), Singapore and Mexico (the other origins Epoch flags)
cust.cn <- c(Malaysia = cv("china", "M", 847150, "Malaysia", "2024-04", "2025-06"), Singapore = cv("china", "M", 847150, "Singapore", "2024-04", "2025-12"),
             Mexico = cv("china", "M", 847150, "Mexico", "2024-10", "2025-09"))
cust.trays <- cv("china", "M", 847180, "Mexico", "2025-03", "2025-07")                   # Mexican-origin "other units of computers"
trays.n <- cv("china", "M", 847180, "Mexico", "2025-03", "2025-07", "qty_units"); trays.kg <- cv("china", "M", 847180, "Mexico", "2025-03", "2025-07", "weight_kg")
## Thailand's own export record: to China above the 2022-23 monthly mean (24 months less 24 at that mean); to Hong Kong (nil before 2024)
cust.th.cn <- cv("thailand", "X", 847150, "China", "2024-01", "2025-12") - cv("thailand", "X", 847150, "China", "2022-01", "2023-12")
cust.th.hk <- cv("thailand", "X", 847150, "Hong Kong", "2024-01", "2025-12")
## Hong Kong's import record by sending place: monthly lines of at least $20M averaging $50,000 a unit or more, from Taiwan and Indonesia, to end-2025.
## Lines sent from Thailand are in cust.th.hk; lines sent from Malaysia are left out, since they may re-enter China as Malaysian origin (cust.cn).
dear <- function(usd, units) ifelse(usd >= 20e6 & units > 0 & usd / units >= 50e3 & hk.c$period <= "2025-12", usd, 0)
cust.hk <- sum(dear(hk.c$M_consigned_TW_usd, hk.c$M_consigned_TW_units)) + sum(dear(hk.c$M_consigned_ID_usd, hk.c$M_consigned_ID_units))
cust <- c("China's record: Malaysian, Singaporean, Mexican servers" = sum(cust.cn), "China's record: Mexican-origin other computer units" = cust.trays,
          "Thailand's record: to China" = cust.th.cn, "Thailand's record: to Hong Kong" = cust.th.hk, "Hong Kong's record: from Taiwan and Indonesia" = cust.hk)
cust.total <- sum(cust); usd.per.h100e <- 25e3                                           # Epoch's conversion for its Malaysian corridor
round(cust / 1e9, 2)                                                                     # US$ billion, to end-2025
## China's record: Malaysian, Singaporean, Mexican servers 
##                                                    5.09 
##     China's record: Mexican-origin other computer units 
##                                                    1.82 
##                             Thailand's record: to China 
##                                                    2.18 
##                         Thailand's record: to Hong Kong 
##                                                    0.81 
##           Hong Kong's record: from Taiwan and Indonesia 
##                                                    1.09
c("total ($bn)" = round(cust.total / 1e9, 1), "H100e at $25,000 (k)" = round(cust.total / usd.per.h100e / 1e3), "share of the end-2025 diverted stock (%)" = round(100 * cust.total / usd.per.h100e / smuggled.2025),
  "China's own entries alone (%)" = round(100 * (sum(cust.cn) + cust.trays) / usd.per.h100e / smuggled.2025))
##                              total ($bn) 
##                                       11 
##                     H100e at $25,000 (k) 
##                                      440 
## share of the end-2025 diverted stock (%) 
##                                       66 
##            China's own entries alone (%) 
##                                       42
  • The law and the buyer’s interest. Receiving and selling these chips was legal in China provided border taxes were paid (Wu and Olcott 2025). A business needs a special VAT invoice to credit the 13% input tax and an invoice to deduct the purchase against income tax (Standing Committee of the National People’s Congress 2024; State Taxation Administration 2018): to a profitable firm, 11.5% and 22.1% of the tax-inclusive price. A firm that sells computing must also invoice its own customers, which puts the revenue, and the servers that earn it, on its books. The buyers reported are data-center operators that rent out computing, and other companies (Wu and Olcott 2025).
  • The customs record. Importers record the country of origin and exporters the destination, so both ends of a shipment are published. By the end of 2025:
    • China’s own import statistics record 5.1bn dollars of servers of Malaysian, Singaporean and Mexican origin in the months they arrived at AI-server prices. The Malaysian part, 3.75bn at about $106,000 a machine against $600 before, is Epoch’s finding; the importers “were breaking no Chinese law, so had less reason to lie to their own customs” (Juniewicz 2026c). China also records 1.8bn of Mexican-origin “other units of computers” in March–July 2025, 16,000 units at about $113,000 and 26 kg each.
    • Thailand records 2.2bn of server exports to China above its 2022–23 level, most of it in March–May 2025, and 0.81bn to Hong Kong. The timing coincides with the largest case charged so far: according to the U.S. Department of Justice, a buyer in Southeast Asia took about $2.5bn of servers, and at least about $510M of them are alleged to have gone on to China between late April and mid-May 2025 (Department of Justice 2026). That this lane is the route in that case is our inference from the timing; the customs record does not show it.
    • Hong Kong records 1.1bn arriving from Taiwan and Indonesia in consignments averaging $50,000 a unit or more (Census and Statistics Department 2026).
    • Together 11bn dollars. At Epoch’s $25,000 per H100e that is 440k H100e, 66% of the end-2025 diverted stock; China’s own entries alone are 42%. The conversion is rough: the values are for whole machines, and newer chips carry more H100e per dollar.
  • How the hardware is sold. On a public brokers’ board in August–October 2026 (Jujianbao 2026), the offers that state tax terms mostly price the goods tax-inclusive or with an invoice, and many cite contracts, bank guarantees or letters of credit. These are offers, not completed sales, and the posters are not verified. On concealing restricted chips inside permitted imports, a trader told the Financial Times: “You can go against the American rules, but not the Chinese” (Olcott 2026a).
  • What is not measured. Small lots: single cards carried by hand or sent under false labels (Huang 2024; Swanson and Fu 2024). They are where a sale without paper is most plausible, and no source sizes them. A record also need not name the chip: invoices often say only “servers”, and the holder of record can be a lessor or a trading company, not the user.

A tenth is left for small lots and for sales without paper; that is a judgment. At a quarter instead, \(K_M(\text{China})\) would be 14k.

Result: \(K_M(s)\) = 12k H100e for the U.S. and 11k for China. Missing failed chips are 4.5k and 1.7k of that, and functional chips 7.5k and 9.6k. The diverted stock accounts for 5.2k of China’s figure.

S.6.6 From the missing stock to the ledger: the scenarios

A state acting in good faith cannot marshal chips its own census failed to find. A state that is hiding chips does so inside that noise, in the mass balance of shipped, declared and removed chips, where hidden chips look like chips the census missed. So the raw dark stock is \(K_0 = (1 + \gamma)\,K_M(s)\), with \(\gamma\) the hidden stock as a multiple of the missing stock, and the ledger counts \(K_E = \pi_E K_0\), \(K_B = \pi_B K_0\). Here \(\pi\) is a rival’s conservative, one-significant-figure estimate of the share of the dark stock the state controls: it cannot tell hidden chips from missing ones, so it rounds the hidden share up. \(\tau_E = \tau_B = 1\): at the pause date the dark stock is young (most of the U.S. residual was bought in 2025–26); aging belongs in a technical discount that declines over a long pause.

hid <- rbind("U.S." = c(0.20, 4), "China" = c(0.20, 9))                        # gamma = hidden stock / K_M: high, low cooperation
K.miss <- c("U.S." = K.miss.us, "China" = K.miss.cn)
dark <- cbind((1 + hid) * K.miss, dark.nd)     # K_0 per state; non-deniable concealment is set politically, as in the paper
colnames(dark) <- scen
pi.dark <- rbind("U.S." = c(0.5, 1, 1), "China" = c(0.5, 1, 1)); dimnames(pi.dark) <- dimnames(dark)   # pi_E = pi_B, tau = 1
K.E.dark <- pi.dark * dark
round(rbind("U.S. K_0 (k)" = dark["U.S.", ] / 1e3, "  pi" = pi.dark["U.S.", ], "  K_E (k)" = K.E.dark["U.S.", ] / 1e3, "  K_E / F_E (%)" = 100 * K.E.dark["U.S.", ] / F.E,
            "  K_B / F_B (%)" = 100 * K.E.dark["U.S.", ] / F.B, "  dark alone: headroom to alpha_E F_E (OOM)" = log10(0.25 * F.E / K.E.dark["U.S.", ]),
            "China K_0 (k)" = dark["China", ] / 1e3, "  pi" = pi.dark["China", ], "  K_E (k)" = K.E.dark["China", ] / 1e3, "  K_E / F_E (%)" = 100 * K.E.dark["China", ] / F.E,
            "  K_B / F_B (%)" = 100 * K.E.dark["China", ] / F.B, "  dark alone: headroom to alpha_E F_E (OOM)" = log10(0.25 * F.E / K.E.dark["China", ])), 3)
##                                             high cooperation low cooperation
## U.S. K_0 (k)                                          14.385          59.937
##   pi                                                   0.500           1.000
##   K_E (k)                                              7.192          59.937
##   K_E / F_E (%)                                        0.113           0.938
##   K_B / F_B (%)                                        0.004           0.034
##   dark alone: headroom to alpha_E F_E (OOM)            2.346           1.426
## China K_0 (k)                                         13.545         112.877
##   pi                                                   0.500           1.000
##   K_E (k)                                              6.773         112.877
##   K_E / F_E (%)                                        0.106           1.767
##   K_B / F_B (%)                                        0.004           0.064
##   dark alone: headroom to alpha_E F_E (OOM)            2.373           1.151
##                                             non-deniable concealment
## U.S. K_0 (k)                                                 300.000
##   pi                                                           1.000
##   K_E (k)                                                    300.000
##   K_E / F_E (%)                                                4.696
##   K_B / F_B (%)                                                0.171
##   dark alone: headroom to alpha_E F_E (OOM)                    0.726
## China K_0 (k)                                               1000.000
##   pi                                                           1.000
##   K_E (k)                                                   1000.000
##   K_E / F_E (%)                                               15.655
##   K_B / F_B (%)                                                0.569
##   dark alone: headroom to alpha_E F_E (OOM)                    0.203
  • Values. High cooperation, the same for both states: a state stashes at most a fifth of its missing stock (\(\gamma\) = 0.2, so \(K_0 = 1.2\,K_M(s)\)), and a rival, to whom the cooperation is evident, counts at most half of the missing compute as in the state’s hands (\(\pi\) = 0.5), so the ledger carries \(0.6\,K_M(s)\). Low cooperation: politically sensitive records are refused and each state holds back what it deniably can, taken as ten times the missing stock for China (\(\gamma\) = 9) and five times for the U.S. (\(\gamma\) = 4), where a large stock would be harder to keep secret; undiscounted (\(\pi\) = 1). These multiples are judgmental inputs. Non-deniable concealment is not a multiple of the missing stock; it keeps the paper’s political sizes, 300k and 1M. At the $25,000 per H100e of §S.1.3 the raw dark stock \(K_0\) is worth about $0.36B in each state under high cooperation, $1.5B (U.S.) and $2.8B (China) under low cooperation, and $7.5B and $25B under non-deniable concealment.
  • High cooperation: \(K_0\) is 14k (U.S.) and 14k (China); the ledger counts 7.2k and 6.8k, 0.11% and 0.11% of \(F_E\). Low cooperation: 60k and 110k, 0.94% and 1.8% of \(F_E\) and 0.034% and 0.064% of \(F_B\).

S.6.7 Judgment calls

  • Direction of conservatism. A larger residual is the regime-unfavorable side. 2.9M is central. Leaving the diverted chips in the “Other” share before applying the location share would give 3.5M, the regime-unfavorable reading, but it would place chips that are in China in the United States.
  • The seven firms’ inventories are presumed accounted for; that presumption, not the residual’s size, carries the argument.
  • Census inputs (§S.6.4–§S.6.6), with the direction of each. Judgments: the location share (0.45), the 2026 growth of the unnamed residual (it keeps its share of world additions), \(v\) = 0.01, the tenth of business-held chips outside a data center and the further 6% missed inside one, the off-books share of diverted chips (a tenth; §S.6.5 gives the evidence), the declaration and recovery rates for off-books and informal holdings (20% undeclared, half recovered), one month of diverted stock in transit split between the two states, the shares of failed chips that leave no record (1% under warranty and a tenth after it at publicly identifiable and on-books holdings, half at off-books holdings, all at informal holdings), the rise of three percentage points a year in the failure rate after year three, and the hidden multiples and discounts (\(\gamma\), \(\pi\)). Analogies, each on the regime-unfavorable side: declaration at the IRS category II rate, tracing at the ATF rate, the share outside a data center for all servers rather than AI servers, and Ascend’s unnamed part counted as tail. Capacity statements of unstated precision count at half.

S.7 The ledger lines (§6.4.2, §6.4.4–§6.4.7)

S.7.1 Transitional training-capable inference service (§6.4.2)

The largest single line on either ledger, early in the regime, is the legacy training-capable fleet left in commercial service through Phases 1 and 2. Its raw size is the fleet measurement of §S.1.2.7 and §S.1.2.8; what this section adds is the discounting.

Under an overt breakout the host state could seize that hardware in industry-grade data centers and run it at full rate, so \(\pi_B = \tau_B = 1\) and the breakout capacity is the fleet itself. Under covert evasion the verification measures of §3.3.3 bite: the U.S. figure assumes pessimistically that 10% of hardware operators evade while diverting 1% of their computing power, which is \(\pi_E = 0.001\); the Chinese figure assumes the state can suborn every operator into diverting 1%, which is \(\pi_E = 0.01\).

pi.E.us <- 0.10 * 0.01; pi.E.cn <- 0.01                                   # 10% of operators x 1% diverted; all operators x 1%
K.trans <- rbind("U.S."  = c(K_0 = us.fleet.ye2026,    K_B = us.fleet.ye2026,    K_E = pi.E.us * us.fleet.ye2026),
                 "China" = c(K_0 = china.fleet.ye2026, K_B = china.fleet.ye2026, K_E = pi.E.cn * china.fleet.ye2026))
round(cbind(K.trans / 1e6, "K_B % of F_B" = 100 * K.trans[, "K_B"] / F.B, "K_E % of F_E" = 100 * K.trans[, "K_E"] / F.E), 3)
##         K_0   K_B   K_E K_B % of F_B K_E % of F_E
## U.S.  35.22 35.22 0.035        20.05        0.551
## China  3.11  3.11 0.031         1.77        0.487

At the adopted \(F_B\) the U.S. transitional fleet is 20% of the breakout fleet and China’s is 1.8%, so both sit inside the allowance \(\alpha_B = 0.25\) of §S.7.5 from entry into force. §S.5.5 shows the conclusion reversing if the breakout target is set on an end-2028 arrival rather than end-2029. On the covert side the discounting does the work: 0.55% of \(F_E\) for the United States and 0.49% for China.

round(rbind("China fleet (M H100e)" = china.range / 1e6, "K_B % of F_B" = 100 * china.range / F.B,
            "K_E % of F_E" = 100 * pi.E.cn * china.range / F.E), 3)
##                         low median  high
## China fleet (M H100e) 2.559  3.111 4.506
## K_B % of F_B          1.457  1.771 2.565
## K_E % of F_E          0.401  0.487 0.705

Across the full range for China’s fleet (§S.1.2.8) the breakout share stays between 1.5% and 2.6% and the covert share under 1% of \(F_E\), an order of magnitude below the U.S. breakout figure throughout. The range moves no qualitative conclusion.

S.7.2 Inference-only accelerators (§6.4.4)

inference.fleet <- 2 / 3 * fleet.ye2026                                  # Deloitte (Crossan et al. 2025): two thirds of AI compute on inference in 2026
pi.E.infonly <- 0.001                                                    # §6.4.4: "as assumed above", the transitional-fleet value
## phi = peak training throughput (H100e) / licensed inference rating (inference-H100e): 1 for a legacy chip, 0 for the idealized inference-only machine
phi.adopted <- 1e-4                                                      # the adopted illustrative residual training factor
phi.cases <- c("phi = 0.01" = 0.01, "phi = 0.001" = 0.001, "phi = 1e-4 (adopted)" = phi.adopted, "phi = 3e-5 (an optimistic case)" = 3e-5)
inf <- sapply(phi.cases, function(f) c("1M of breakout ledger serves (M H100e of demand)" = 1e6 / f / 1e6, "K_B: world inference replicated 100x (k H100e)" = 100 * inference.fleet * f / 1e3,
                                       "  ... as % of F_B" = 100 * 100 * inference.fleet * f / F.B, "K_E = pi_E x K_B (k H100e)" = pi.E.infonly * 100 * inference.fleet * f / 1e3,
                                       "  ... as % of F_E" = 100 * pi.E.infonly * 100 * inference.fleet * f / F.E))
signif(inf, 3)

##                                             0.099 
##        phi = 0.001 in TFLOP/s per inference-H100e 
##                                             0.989

  • The residual training factor \(\varphi\) is a hardware system’s peak arithmetic throughput for training operations, in H100e, divided by its licensed inference rating, in inference-H100e. A legacy training-capable chip has \(\varphi = 1\) and the idealized inference-only machine has \(\varphi = 0\); a system hobbled by four orders of magnitude has \(\varphi = 10^{-4}\). The inference rating is known and the residual training throughput is what an inspector bounds from above, so a certified bound on a system is an upper bound on its \(\varphi\).

  • A fleet’s \(\varphi\) is its total training throughput divided by its total inference rating, which is the mean of its units’ \(\varphi\) weighted by inference-H100e. The fleet’s training capacity is then the inference it serves times \(\varphi\), which is what the ledger uses, and a ceiling on every unit’s \(\varphi\) is a ceiling on the fleet’s.

  • The adopted residual training factor is \(\varphi = 10^{-4}\), an illustrative design target as in the paper (§6.4.4): one order of magnitude below \(10^{-3}\) and well above the optimistic case of \(3\times10^{-5}\) shown below. The value is illustrative, and the conclusions do not rest on it. The inference-only line is the inference served times \(\varphi\), so the regime sets the size of the line through the amount of inference-only service it licenses: if certified hardware reached only \(\varphi = 10^{-3}\), licensing a tenth as much inference-only service would leave the line where it is. The first row of the table gives the inference demand that one million H100e of breakout ledger serves at each \(\varphi\). (With a hundred times today’s inference served at \(10^{-3}\), the line alone would be 1.8% of \(F_B\).)

  • \(\pi_E = 0.001\) (§6.4.4: “as assumed above owing to the difficulty of evading discovery by the recomputation server”, i.e. the transitional-fleet value of §6.4.2). At the adopted \(\varphi\), \(K_E\) = 313 H100e = 0.0049% of \(F_E\).

  • The optimistic case. At \(\varphi = 3\times10^{-5}\), replicating the world’s inference a hundred times over costs about 94k H100e of breakout ledger, 0.05% of \(F_B\).

  • The two-thirds inference share is market-wide. It need not match a frontier lab’s own split: the SemiAnalysis model cited in §S.1.1.4 has inference at 36–38% of the combined capacity of OpenAI and Anthropic (Xie et al. 2026). The two differ because they describe different populations.

  • The inference fleet is 31M on the world model (§6.4.4); \(K_B\) at the adopted \(\varphi\) is 313k H100e, 0.18% of \(F_B\) (at \(\varphi = 10^{-3}\) it would be 3.1M and 1.8%).

S.7.3 Consumer GPUs (§6.4.5, fn 72–73)

K0.consumer <- h100e(100e6 * 30e12); tau.consumer <- 0.10; pi.B.consumer <- 0.25
round(c("fn 72: Q2 2026 desktop add-in boards, JPR (M)" = 12.5, "fn 72: laptop residual = 20M - 12.5M (M)" = 20 - 12.5, "K_0 = 100M cards x 30 TFLOP/s (M H100e)" = K0.consumer / 1e6,
        "K_E = 0.01 x tau x K_0 (k)" = 0.01 * tau.consumer * K0.consumer / 1e3, "  ... % of F_E" = 100 * 0.01 * tau.consumer * K0.consumer / F.E,
        "K_B = 0.25 x tau x K_0 (k)" = pi.B.consumer * tau.consumer * K0.consumer / 1e3, "  ... % of F_B" = 100 * pi.B.consumer * tau.consumer * K0.consumer / F.B), 3)
## fn 72: Q2 2026 desktop add-in boards, JPR (M) 
##                                        12.500 
##      fn 72: laptop residual = 20M - 12.5M (M) 
##                                         7.500 
##       K_0 = 100M cards x 30 TFLOP/s (M H100e) 
##                                         3.033 
##                    K_E = 0.01 x tau x K_0 (k) 
##                                         3.033 
##                                  ... % of F_E 
##                                         0.047 
##                    K_B = 0.25 x tau x K_0 (k) 
##                                        75.834 
##                                  ... % of F_B 
##                                         0.043

The overt political discount is \(\pi_B = 0.25\): a state marshalling hobbyist and gaming cards for an overt program would recover at most a quarter of them. The covert discount is \(\pi_E = 0.01\). The 12.5M in the paper’s footnote 72 is the reported shipment figure for the second quarter of 2026 (Jon Peddie Research 2026); nothing downstream depends on it, since \(K_0\) rests on the rounded bound of 100M cards. The technical discount is \(\tau_E = \tau_B = 0.10\), twice the usefulness factor of about 0.05 that the AI 2040 compute supplement assigns to gaming GPUs (memory bandwidth near 1.0 TB/s against the H100’s 3.35, and 64 Gb/s networking against a 400 Gb/s threshold; Dean 2026a). Doubling it is the regime-unfavorable margin. fn 73 cites NVIDIA (2021) for GeForce cards halving FP16 throughput with FP32 accumulation.

S.7.4 El Capitan and the remaining carve-outs (§6.4.6–6.4.7)

K0.elcap <- h100e(46e3 * 980.6e12)
round(c("K_0 = 46k APUs x 980.6 TFLOP/s (k H100e)" = K0.elcap / 1e3, "K_B = K_0 (tau = pi_B = 1), % of F_B" = 100 * K0.elcap / F.B,
        "K_E = 0.2 x K_0 (k H100e)" = 0.2 * K0.elcap / 1e3, "  ... % of F_E" = 100 * 0.2 * K0.elcap / F.E, "HPL-MxP utilization 37% relative to U_F (tau, capped at 1)" = min(1, 0.37 / U.F)), 2)
##                   K_0 = 46k APUs x 980.6 TFLOP/s (k H100e) 
##                                                      45.61 
##                       K_B = K_0 (tau = pi_B = 1), % of F_B 
##                                                       0.03 
##                                  K_E = 0.2 x K_0 (k H100e) 
##                                                       9.12
